name: Five American World War II conscientious objectors imprisoned for draft resistance

prisoner.name: Howard Schoenfeld
prisoner.description: Howard Schoenfeld was an American fiction writer, editor, and pacifist who resisted conscription before the United States entered World War II. He was prosecuted in New York for refusing to register under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940. His constitutional challenge to peacetime conscription was considered with those of other defendants in United States v. Rappeport in January 1941. Schoenfeld was imprisoned at the federal correctional institution in Danbury, Connecticut, and later described the experience in The Danbury Story. His literary work included science fiction, fantasy, and the crime novel Let Them Eat Bullets.

cases.charges: Failure to register under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940.
cases.sentence: Federal imprisonment at Danbury for conscientious draft resistance is documented. Exact sentence, imprisonment endpoints, and time served have not been verified. January 21, 1941 is the date of a ruling on the constitutional challenge, not an established conviction, sentencing, or release date.

sources.supports: United States v. Rappeport, 36 F. Supp. 915 (S.D.N.Y. January 21, 1941): Howard named among defendants charged with failure to register; constitutional challenge.
Footnote 11 and bibliography identify Schoenfeld's account of conscientious-objector imprisonment at Danbury.
Literary identity, 1915-2004 lifespan, Hot Springs origin, author/editor, and Let Them Eat Bullets (1954).
Page 7 caption identifies Howard as second from left in a four-defendant photograph. Newspaper publication date does not establish photo exposure or arrest date.

entries.research_limits: January 2, 1915 and September 26, 2004 appear in secondary bibliographic results, including an indexed ISFDB excerpt on IDCrawl, but the original ISFDB record and Villager obituary could not be read. Store confirmed lifespan years at year precision pending stronger verification. A contemporary group photo was verified, but no standalone portrait is supplied; unrelated doctors, accountants, and later obituaries were rejected. The reported eleven-month prison term and seven-month parole camp remain unverified and are not encoded.

prisoner.name: James Ellery Bristol
prisoner.description: James Ellery Bristol was an American peace activist and Lutheran minister who was imprisoned for conscientious objection during World War II. He had served a congregation in Camden, New Jersey, and declined a ministerial exemption from military service. Federal records date his conviction to October 31, 1941; he was released in 1943. He later joined the American Friends Service Committee and directed its Quaker Center in New Delhi, helping organize and accompany Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King's 1959 visit to India. He remained active in opposition to conscription and war. His draft-law conviction was pardoned in December 1947.

cases.charges: Violation of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 arising from conscientious refusal of military service; exact count unverified.
cases.convicted: Convicted October 31, 1941, U.S. District Court for New Jersey. Pardoned December 23, 1947, by Presidential Proclamation 2762.
cases.sentence: Imprisoned for conscientious draft resistance and released in 1943. Stanford's King Institute reports 18 months served; an AFSC account reports 19 months. The discrepancy is unresolved, so no numeric duration is entered. Exact sentence, prison, arrest date, and release day remain unverified. The 1947 pardon was later than his release.

sources.supports: Full name; DOB 1912-02-12; DOD 1992-10-26; Camden ministry; prison for WWII objection; 1943 release; 18-month account; AFSC and 1959 India trip.
Declined ministerial exemption; AFSC colleague reports 19 months in prison, conflicting with Stanford's 18 months.

prisoner.name: Lee Donald Stern
prisoner.description: Lee Donald Stern was an American Quaker pacifist imprisoned during World War II after refusing to report for Civilian Public Service. He was convicted in northern Ohio in December 1942 and held at the federal prison in Milan, Michigan, from December 1942 through January 1946. In prison he challenged racial segregation by eating with Black prisoners. He later taught nonviolence and conflict resolution, worked with the Fellowship of Reconciliation, and helped found Alternatives to Violence and Peace Brigades International. His draft-law conviction was pardoned in December 1947.

cases.charges: Failure to report for Civilian Public Service as a conscientious objector under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940.
cases.convicted: Convicted December 7, 1942, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio. Pardoned December 23, 1947, by Presidential Proclamation 2762.
cases.sentence: Swarthmore's Lee Stern Papers describe imprisonment at Milan from December 1942 through January 1946. The exact sentence and individual entry and release days are unverified; dates are stored at month precision. December 7 is a verified conviction date, not an independently verified prison admission date.

prisoner.name: Robert Swann
prisoner.description: Robert Swann was an American peace activist and community land trust pioneer. A conscientious objector during World War II, he refused to cooperate with the draft and was imprisoned at the Federal Correctional Institution in Ashland, Kentucky. His autobiography dates that imprisonment from September 1942 to September 1944 and describes serving two years of a five-year sentence. In prison, he studied economics and nonviolent social change with other conscientious objectors. He later helped establish New Communities in Georgia and became founding president of the Schumacher Center for a New Economics.
affiliation: Schumacher Center for a New Economics

cases.charges: Refusal to cooperate with the World War II draft as a conscientious objector; exact statutory count unverified.
cases.sentence: Swann's autobiography states a five-year sentence, with two years served at Ashland from September 1942 to September 1944. This firsthand account is used over an obituary reporting a two-and-a-half-year sentence. Exact arrest, sentencing, admission, and release days remain unverified.

sources.supports: Firsthand account: September 1942 arrival at Ashland; September 1944 release; two years of five-year sentence. Month precision, not guessed first-of-month dates.
Full birth/death dates, portrait, New Communities work, founding Schumacher role.

prisoner.name: Donald Earl Wetzel
prisoner.description: Donald Earl Wetzel was an American novelist, humanist, and antiwar activist imprisoned for conscientious draft resistance during World War II. Initially assigned to the Quaker-run Civilian Public Service camp at Big Flats, New York, he left because he believed cooperation with the draft violated his conscience. His prison memoir describes detention on West Street in Manhattan and transfers through Rochester, Chillicothe, and Ashland. He later wrote Pacifist: Or, My War and Louis Lepke. His novels included A Wreath and a Curse, which was adapted for Broadway as All Summer Long, and he received a Guggenheim fellowship.

cases.charges: Conscientious refusal to cooperate with the draft after leaving Civilian Public Service at Big Flats, New York; exact statutory count unverified.
cases.sentence: Imprisonment followed refusal of Civilian Public Service. The memoir excerpt in Peter Brock's These Strange Criminals describes West Street detention in Manhattan, then Rochester, Chillicothe, and Ashland. Ashland is the linked institution, not a claim that all custody occurred there. Exact dates and total time served are unverified; CPS camp service is not counted as imprisonment.

sources.supports: Arizona Daily Star death notice, June 27, 2007: full name, DOB 1921-06-08, DOD 2007-06-21; novelist and humanist identity.
Donald Wetzel chapter: conscientious CPS walkout, imprisonment and transfer sequence; firsthand memoir excerpt.
